subject: Communication
title: Reframing: Changing the Lens
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Reframing: Changing the Lens.

hook.text: 'He's lazy and doesn't care.' Reframed: 'He seems overwhelmed. What support does he need?' Same person. Different story.

buildup.text: Reframing transforms conflict by changing how the situation is described — without changing the facts.

discovery.text: Mediators reframe accusations into needs: 'She never listens' becomes 'You need to feel heard.'

twist.text: Reframing isn't spinning or minimizing. It's finding the legitimate need hiding behind the hostile expression.

climax.text: Once a conflict is reframed from 'us vs. them' to 'us vs. the problem,' collaborative solutions emerge naturally.

punchline.text: Change the frame and the entire conflict changes with it.

quiz.question: What is the goal of reframing in mediation?

details.summary: Reframing reinterprets a statement or situation to shift its meaning without changing the facts. In conflict, a mediator might reframe 'He never listens to me' as 'You really value being heard.' This technique moves conversations from blame to needs.
details.whyItMatters: Reframing is the mediator's most versatile tool. By changing the lens, you open paths to resolution that were invisible before.
takeaways: Reframing changes interpretation without changing facts
It shifts focus from blame to underlying needs
Mediators and therapists use it as a core technique

faq.question: What is the difference between reframing and minimizing?
faq.answer: Reframing changes the interpretation while respecting the experience. Minimizing dismisses or trivializes it. Saying 'You value being heard' honors the need. Saying 'It's not that big a deal' minimizes the pain. Effective reframing always validates before redirecting.

faq.question: Can you reframe your own thoughts during conflict?
faq.answer: Absolutely. Internal reframing is a core cognitive behavioral technique. Instead of thinking 'She's attacking me,' reframe to 'She's frustrated about the situation.' This shift reduces defensive reactions and opens you to hearing what is actually being said.
